title: Academic foundations
lede: What any school model has to move. Math was hit hardest and is recovering fastest, but the average hides a split: top students have regained their footing while the lowest performers keep sliding to record lows on both NAEP and TIMSS. PISA 2025 adds a second reading of the same story: U.S. scores held roughly where they were in 2022 while the OECD fell sharply, so the United States now looks average by standing still. Alongside the academic core, states are writing durable skills into graduation expectations without an agreed way to measure them.

kpis.label: Grade 8 math, 10th percentile score
kpis.note: Down 5 more points since 2022 while the 90th percentile rose 3 (to 328).

kpis.label: Grade 4 math, NAEP average
kpis.note: The only national gain on the 2024 Report Card; driven by middle- and higher-performing students. Alabama is the lone state above its 2019 level.

kpis.label: Grade 8 math, TIMSS
kpis.note: Lowest U.S. score since TIMSS began in 1995; 19 of 45 systems scored higher. Grade 4 fell 18 points to 517.

kpis.label: Seniors below NAEP Basic in math
kpis.note: 22% at or above Proficient (−2). 33% of seniors were prepared for entry-level college math, down from 37%.

kpis.label: States with math laws or policies since 2022
kpis.note: Screening (13 states) and intervention (11) lead; 10 states auto-enroll qualifying students in advanced math.

kpis.label: Schools offering Algebra I by 8th grade
kpis.note: Where offered, over half of Asian students enroll versus 22% of Latino and 17% of Black students.

chart.title: Grade 8 math by percentile, 2019 to 2024
chart.subtitle: NAEP scale scores. The lowest performers lost the most and kept losing after 2022; the top has nearly recovered.
chart.note: Between 2022 and 2024 the 90th and 75th percentiles rose 3 and 2 points while the 10th and 25th fell 5 and 3. The gap between the 90th and 10th percentiles is now 109 points.

items.label: 8th graders at or above NAEP Proficient in math
items.note: 8% reached Advanced. But only 61% are at or above Basic, down 1 point: the middle is hollowing.

items.label: 4th graders below NAEP Basic in math
items.note: 'Nearly a quarter' likely cannot identify odd numbers or solve a unit-conversion problem; nearly 40% are Proficient or Advanced.

items.label: TIMSS grade 4 math, 10th-percentile change since 2019
items.note: Lowest in the assessment's 30-year history; the 90th percentile did not change. 18% of 8th graders fell below the Low international benchmark.

items.label: TIMSS gender gap in 8th-grade math
items.note: First significant 8th-grade math gap since 2003; boys outscored girls in both subjects and grades.

chart.title: TIMSS math, U.S. average scores
chart.subtitle: International benchmark (centerpoint 500); the axis starts at 470, not zero. Both grades posted their lowest U.S. scores ever in 2023.
chart.note: Singapore led both grades (fourth grade up to 615; eighth grade 605). Twenty-one of 63 systems beat the U.S. at grade 4; 19 of 45 at grade 8.

chart.title: Top-quintile 8th graders enrolled in algebra
chart.subtitle: Among the highest-achieving fifth of students in schools that offer 8th-grade algebra, by race/ethnicity.
chart.note: Opt-in placement that relies on teacher recommendation or parent advocacy under-enrolls Black, Latino and low-income students; ten states now auto-enroll students who test at grade level.

blocks.title: PISA 2025: the U.S. result
blocks.subtitle: U.S. 15-year-olds, released September 8, 2026. Scores are on the PISA scale and are not comparable to NAEP or TIMSS scales.

items.label: Mathematics, U.S. average
items.unit: not significantly different from the OECD average
items.note: Among the 38 OECD member countries the U.S. scored lower than 14 and higher than 7. U.S. math and reading results are below 2018 and among the lowest observed for the United States in PISA.

items.label: Reading, U.S. average
items.note: Still well above the OECD average, but the U.S. decline since 2018 runs in the same direction as the international one.

items.label: Science, U.S. average
items.note: Science was the focal domain in 2025 and is the one subject where the U.S. result is clearly above the OECD average.

items.label: U.S. students below baseline proficiency in math
items.note: Roughly one in three 15-year-olds cannot reliably use mathematics in a straightforward applied situation, against one in twelve working at the top two levels.

blocks.title: PISA 2025: the OECD picture
blocks.subtitle: Why the U.S. position improved relative to peers without U.S. scores improving.

items.label: OECD average reading change, 2015 to 2025
items.unit: points, about one and a half years of learning
items.note: Reading and mathematics both reached their lowest OECD averages on record.

items.label: OECD average mathematics change, 2015 to 2025
items.unit: points, just over one year of learning
items.note: Science was flat between 2022 and 2025 after trending down from 2009, so the collapse is specific to reading and math.

items.label: OECD students who are low performers in all three subjects
items.note: The share failing to reach baseline across every subject rose by about four points in three years.

items.label: Students assessed
items.note: Across OECD countries, advantaged students outscored disadvantaged students by 85 points in science; the gap narrowed since 2022 mainly because advantaged students did worse.

chart.title: What state math laws require
chart.subtitle: Number of states (of 22) whose post-2022 math laws or policies include each element.
chart.note: Alabama's 2022 Numeracy Act set the template: K-2 screeners, coaches, approved curricula and 60 minutes of daily math. Actions by year: 1 (2022), 6 (2023), 1 (2024), 7 (2025), 9 (2026).

items.headline: Math bounced back first.
items.detail: After the pandemic, math achievement rebounded immediately and the annual rate of improvement returned to pre-2013 levels in 2022–2024, while reading kept declining through 2024.

items.headline: Absenteeism drags math harder than reading.
items.detail: Across 2,000 districts, high-absenteeism districts were about 50% further from recovery in math than in reading.

items.headline: Grade-level readiness is barely moving.
items.detail: Among nearly 14 million i-Ready students, the share meeting grade-level benchmarks has been flat since spring 2023 with only a slight uptick by spring 2025; early grades and lower performers remain furthest behind.

items.headline: Texas shows what acceleration looks like.
items.detail: In 2026, 54% of Algebra I test-takers met grade level (+7 points), and 32% of 7th graders took the grade-8 math STAAR, double the 16% of 2023.

items.headline: Secondary math is the next frontier.
items.detail: Fractions and fluency with basic operations are the concepts that most trip up middle and high schoolers, per an EdWeek survey of 729 educators; state policy has so far concentrated on K-5.

items.headline: The SAT shows math recovering but not recovered.
items.detail: The class of 2026 averaged 1045 on the SAT, up 16 points and the second consecutive year of gains, with increases across every demographic group. Reading and writing rose 7 points to 528, back to pre-pandemic levels; math rose 9 points to 517 and is still below the 523 of the 2020 cohort. Forty-two percent of takers met both college and career readiness benchmarks, out of nearly 2 million students tested.

items.headline: Standing still was enough to move up internationally.
items.detail: U.S. PISA math and science results in 2025 were about the same as 2022 while OECD averages fell to their lowest recorded levels in math and reading. A model benchmarked against international peers should be careful here: the relative gain is a fall elsewhere, not a U.S. improvement, and U.S. math remains below its own 2018 level.

blocks.title: What moves achievement inside a school
blocks.subtitle: Interventions that run inside an existing school, as opposed to a redesign of the school itself. Effect sizes are in standard deviations and are quoted with the study that produced them; they are not comparable across different outcomes and populations.

cells: High-dosage in-school tutoring (Chicago and Fulton County, 2022–23)
≈2,000 students in districtwide programs; University of Chicago Education Lab
About two-thirds of a year of additional math learning, enough to offset the pandemic loss for the average student. Delivery during the school day was critical.
Saga two-on-one daily math tutoring (Chicago high schools)
Multiple RCTs published in the American Economic Review
0.16–0.37 SD on math test scores, plus lower course-failure rates; effects shrink as programs scale.
Khanmigo AI tutor in daily remedial math (Tennessee)
Two-year cluster RCT, 18 middle schools (NBER, 2026)
0.06–0.08 SD per year of assignment; up to 0.14 SD with a full year of active use. Similar to Khan practice without AI; engagement is the binding constraint.
AI assistance on math and reading tasks (Liu et al., 2026)
Three randomized experiments, 1,222 participants
Higher assisted performance, then lower persistence and unassisted performance: students finish faster and learn less.
Generative AI on ALEKS math problems (Rismanchian et al., 2026)
Quasi-experimental analysis of 3.2 million student interactions
Students who used generative AI spent less time on problems and built less of the knowledge the problems are designed to teach.
Human tutors with an AI copilot (Stanford)
RCT, 1,800 K-12 students
+4 percentage points mastery; +9 for students of less-experienced tutors.
Ampact (Reading Corps)
AmeriCorps literacy tutors embedded in K-3 classrooms, working with 15 to 18 students for 20 minutes each a day
Two randomized studies with 798 students; average effect +0.36 SD, reaching +0.74 on letter-sound fluency in the Minnesota trial
Chapter One
Part-time tutors push into kindergarten classrooms for 5 to 10 minute bursts during reading blocks, rather than pulling students out
Two randomized studies with 1,009 students; average effect +0.23 SD, and +0.31 on the district reading level assessment in the larger trial
Saga Education
In-school math tutoring for ninth and tenth graders, at least three times a week, at ratios between one to two and one to four
Three randomized trials with 5,396 students; average effect +0.14 SD, with per-study effects of +0.09, +0.14 and +0.19 for students assigned to tutoring
Reading Partners
Community volunteers tutor students in grades 2 to 5 one-to-one, twice a week, in a dedicated reading center inside the school
One large randomized trial by MDRC with 1,166 students; effect +0.10 SD on comprehension, against a control group that mostly received other literacy support

items.note: Fastest-growing AP course; 81% scored 3 or higher in 2025 (76% in 2024).

items.label: AP Calculus exam takers, 2025
items.note: Calculus AB 285,891 and BC 160,436. Black students are 8% of Precalculus takers vs 5% of Calc AB; Hispanic students 23% vs 17%.

items.label: Seniors academically prepared for college math
items.note: Yet more seniors report acceptance to a four-year college than in 2019.

items.label: States reporting math teacher shortages
items.note: Among the three most common shortage areas nationally, alongside special education and science.

items.label: Job postings requiring at least one durable skill
items.note: America Succeeds' analysis of postings; the share asking for three or more rose 13%. Durable skills are communication, collaboration, critical thinking and similar.

items.label: States turning graduate portraits into policy
items.note: North Carolina and Indiana are furthest along in actually teaching and assessing durable skills rather than only declaring them.

items.label: North Carolina's portrait against employer demand
items.note: A state commerce department analysis found projected employment growth is higher in occupations that place the most importance on durable skills.

items.label: Agreed measure of durable skills
items.note: No state assesses durable skills the way it assesses reading and math, so a model claiming to build them cannot yet be held to it.
